props.title: Liliom

sections.content: Fritz Lang's **Liliom** (1934) marks a fascinating bridge between German Expressionism and French Poetic Realism. Made during Lang's brief stay in France before fleeing to Hollywood, this adaptation of Ferenc Molnár's 1909 play showcases the director's masterful blend of supernatural elements with gritty realism. The film shares DNA with later works like **It's A Wonderful Life** (1946) and **A Matter of Life and Death** (1946) in its exploration of the afterlife through a distinctly humanist lens. Charles Boyer delivers a compelling performance as the titular carousel barker whose journey extends beyond death.

sections.content: The film's influence on French Poetic Realism cannot be overstated. Directors like Marcel Carné, whose **Le Jour Se Lève** (1939) and **Children of Paradise** (1945) would define the movement, clearly drew inspiration from Lang's melding of fatalistic themes with working-class settings. The carnival setting and doomed romance anticipate later works like **The Seventh Seal** (1957), while the celestial bureaucracy sequences influenced everything from **Here Comes Mr. Jordan** (1941) to **Defending Your Life** (1991). SUBHEAD: Expressionist Techniques in French Cinema

Lang's expressionist touches - particularly in the heavenly judgment sequences - demonstrate how German film techniques infiltrated French cinema of the 1930s. The stark lighting and geometrical compositions recall his earlier works like **Metropolis** (1927) and **M** (1931), while pointing toward the film noir style he would help establish in Hollywood with **Scarlet Street** (1945) and **The Woman in the Window** (1944). The film's innovative special effects, particularly in depicting the afterlife, established a visual language for representing the supernatural that influenced decades of cinema.
